input:
Sampling a gas emission representatively is a more subtle exercise than it might first appear. This passage explains where samples should be taken, how increments combine to form one sample, and why a single grab sample can mislead; together these points let a sampling visit be planned and its results read with appropriate confidence.

The sampling position comes first. The sample should be taken at a sampling plane across the duct, at a section where the flow has settled: downstream of bends, fans, and junctions by a clear length of straight duct, and upstream of any point where gas enters or leaves. At that plane the probe should be moved across the section during the run, because gas composition and flow are rarely uniform across a duct: the centre runs faster than the edges, and where droplets or solids are carried, their distribution across the section is uneven as well. A probe fixed at the wall samples the edge of the stream, not the stream.

A sample is then built up from increments. An increment is a single portion of gas drawn at one position and one time; the sample sent for analysis is the combination of many increments taken across the plane and across the whole period the measurement covers. The sampling plan for the source sets how many increments are taken and how they are spaced, and the spacing follows the way the emission varies: closer together where the process cycles quickly, wider apart where it runs steadily. The analysed sample thus has the composition of the period, averaged in the proportions the period produced.

A single grab sample misleads because it freezes one moment of a moving quantity: an emission rises and falls with load, with batch steps, and with cleaning and start-up, and a grab taken at a quiet moment reports the quiet moment. The analysis of the bottle may be exact, yet the result is still wrong for the period the grab is taken to represent, because the gas in the bottle is the gas of one moment only. Increments spread across the period average that movement into the sample: the analysed gas matches the gas the whole period discharged, which is what a representative sample means.

Choose the sampling position first. The sample is taken at a sampling plane across the duct, at a section where the flow has settled: downstream of bends, fans, and junctions by a clear length of straight duct, and upstream of any point where gas enters or leaves. At that plane, move the probe across the section during the run. Gas composition and flow are rarely uniform across a duct: the centre runs faster than the edges, and and carried droplets or solids are unevenly distributed. A probe fixed at the wall samples the edge of the stream, not the stream.

Build one sample from increments. An increment is a single portion of gas drawn at one position and one time; the sample that goes for analysis is the combination of many increments taken across the plane and across the whole measured period. The sampling plan for the source sets how many increments are taken and how they are spaced, and the spacing follows the emission's own variation: increments stand closer together where the process cycles quickly and wider apart where it runs steadily. The analysed sample then has the composition of the period as a whole.

A single grab sample misleads because it freezes one moment of a moving quantity. An emission rises and falls with load, with batch steps, with cleaning and start-up, and a grab taken at a quiet moment reports the quiet moment. The analysis of the bottle may be exact, and the result is still wrong for the period the grab is taken to represent, because the gas in the bottle is the gas of one moment only. Increments spread across the period average that movement into the sample. A representative sample means that match: the analysed gas has the composition of the gas the whole period discharged.
